title: Where fame was born
hook: Two million notable lives, from 3500 BC to 2018: where they began, and where they ended.
notes: Laouenan, Bhargava, Eymeoud, Gergaud, Plique and Wasmer (2022), 'A cross-verified database of notable people, 3500BC–2018AD', Scientific Data 9:290; data.sciencespo doi:10.21410/7E4/RDAG3O (codes: doi:10.21410/7E4/YLG6YR). The record's terms say CC BY-SA 4.0, the licence file shipped with it CC BY-NC-SA 4.0; we follow the stricter one. The database merges Wikipedia (7 language editions, plus others for counts) and Wikidata, so it counts people someone wrote about, not everyone who mattered: Europe and men are over-represented, and recent births are still being added. Of 2.29 million people, 1.65 million have both a birth year and a birthplace; these are mapped in 0.5° cells and counted per city when born within 25 km of a Natural Earth populated place (modern names). Eras are labelled by their first year. The centre of gravity is the average position of all birthplaces of an era. Born vs died uses only the 633,000 people with both places known. Gender shares count men and women with a recorded gender. Citizenship comparisons use the database’s first recorded citizenship, not verified passports or a representative sample of the population.

scenes.title: Two million lives
scenes.text: Researchers combined Wikipedia and Wikidata into a list of 2.3 million notable people, from 3500 BC to 2018. For 1.65 million we know when and where they were born. The map glows where the record is thickest: Europe and North America. Among people born since 1950 with a recorded citizenship in this database, roughly two-thirds have a European, US or Canadian first citizenship.

layers.title: Notable people born per 0.5° cell, 3500 BC–2018

scenes.title: Cities of fame
scenes.text: Move through the eras. Fame starts around the Mediterranean, then shifts to Italy, Paris and London, and in the 20th century to New York and Los Angeles.

captions.-3499: Before 500 BC: only 130 people with a known birthplace. Athens, Rome and Jerusalem lead.
captions.-499: 500 BC to the birth of Christ: Rome (340) is far ahead of Athens (80).
captions.1: AD 1–499: Rome, Alexandria, Constantinople (today's Istanbul) and Antioch.
captions.500: AD 500–999: the largest centres are in the Islamic world: Mecca, Medina and Baghdad, with Constantinople. Xi’an and Córdoba follow.
captions.1300: 1300–1499: Florence (460) is the capital of fame, ahead of Venice and Milan.
captions.1500: The 1500s: Florence, Antwerp, Paris, Venice, London.
captions.1600: The 1600s: Paris takes the lead it will keep for two centuries.
captions.1800: 1800–1849: Paris, London and Berlin. New York appears.
captions.1975: Born 1975–2018: London, Paris, New York, Los Angeles, Buenos Aires and Tokyo.

layers.title: Notable people born in the city

scenes.title: The centre drifts west
scenes.text: Average the recorded birthplaces of each era and you get a centre of gravity. It starts in Anatolia, swings north of the Black Sea, then crosses Europe: Bavaria in the 1300s, Belgium by 1700. As American birthplaces enter the record it moves into the Atlantic, then east again among people born in 1975–2018. Separately, the share recorded with an Asian first citizenship rises from 11% for births in 1950–1974 to 16% in 1975–2018.

scenes.title: The pull of the capital
scenes.text: Fame often ends in the capital. Compare where people were born with where they died.

options.label: Born here
options.text: Among people whose places of birth and death are both known, 18,000 were born in Paris, 4,100 in Rome and 2,200 in Madrid.

options.label: Died here
options.text: Twice as many died in Paris (36,000) as were born there, nearly three times as many in Rome (12,000) and Madrid (5,900). London is milder: 12,000 born, 14,500 died. Across the Atlantic, Washington counts four times as many deaths as births, and Los Angeles more than five times.

scenes.title: Women enter the record
scenes.text: From 1500 to the 1830s, only about one notable person in 15 was a woman. The share rose from the mid-1800s and reached a quarter for people born in the 1970s and 1980s. Among people born since 1950 it is over a third in China, Taiwan and Ethiopia, 32% in Sweden and South Korea, and lowest in Saudi Arabia (6%) and Qatar (4%).
